title: Search And Intersection
notes: Open by naming the chapter's shift in scale. Earlier chapters used local predicates to classify one turn, one edge, or one cell; this lecture asks what those predicates return when many objects, special cases, and search structures are present. Keep the manifest source span visible as printed pages 220-293, with PDF provenance recorded separately.

title: Source Map And Learning Arc
notes: Use the map as the lecture contract. The chapter begins with pairwise intersection, then lifts the same classification habit to triangles, polygons, segment sets, extremal queries, and planar point location. Emphasize that the PDF provenance is printed page plus nine: pages 220-293 correspond to PDF pages 229-302.

title: From Boolean Predicate To Classified Event
notes: Pause on the distinction between yes-or-no and useful output. For downstream geometry, an intersection routine should explain what happened: proper crossing, endpoint contact, overlapping edge, or miss. That richer event vocabulary is what lets polygon containment, clipping, and search structures agree about boundary cases.

title: Parametric Segment Intersection
notes: Introduce the parameter square before discussing code. Each segment contributes one parameter, and the intersection is valid exactly when both parameters land in the closed unit interval. This turns geometry into a constrained solve, while parallel and nearly parallel directions become visible as denominator warnings.

title: Return Codes In Four Cases
notes: Use the checked artifact as a compact test board. The four cases deliberately include a proper crossing, endpoint touch, collinear overlap, and a miss. Point out that all four are correct outcomes, and collapsing them into one Boolean would lose information needed later by polygon and boundary logic.

title: Degeneracy And Numeric Caution
notes: Treat robustness as part of the specification, not an implementation afterthought. The determinant and parameter formulas are simple, but zero denominators, collinear intervals, and roundoff near zero decide which branch is taken. Students should leave with the habit of documenting an epsilon or exact-arithmetic policy.

title: Segment-Plane Then Triangle
notes: Frame segment-triangle intersection as two nested tests. First intersect the segment with the triangle's supporting plane; only after that do we ask whether the point lies inside the triangular region. The notebook check provides the plane parameter and a concrete intersection point for the class to inspect.

title: Barycentric Classification
notes: Use the barycentric diagram to make classification visual. Inside means all three weights are nonnegative and sum to one; an edge hit has one zero weight; a vertex hit has two zero weights. This is the triangle analogue of returning a classified segment event instead of a bare Boolean.

title: Containment By Ray Parity
notes: Explain ray parity as a crossing-count certificate. A query is inside a polygon when a generic ray crosses the boundary an odd number of times, and outside when the count is even. The checked inside query has three hits, while the outside query has none; degeneracies again require a convention.

title: Convex Polygon Intersection
notes: Present convex polygon intersection as a maintained candidate region. Each clipping line removes a half-plane, so the result remains convex, and the notebook check reports a nonempty seven-vertex intersection with area about 3.232. This slide links local edge tests to an actual output polygon.

title: When There Are Many Segments
notes: Shift from one pair of segments to a set of segments. A sweep line keeps a status order of active segments, because possible intersections are discovered locally among neighbors as the sweep advances. The key teaching point is that global intersection search becomes a sequence of ordered local updates.

title: Support Queries In A Convex Polygon
notes: Define support as an optimization query over vertices. Given a direction vector, the answer is the vertex maximizing the dot product with that direction. The notebook artifact checks four directions and confirms that the highlighted support values are maxima, which prepares students for hierarchical extremal search.

title: Hierarchy Shrinkage
notes: Make the hierarchy quantitative. The stored levels shrink from 72 vertices to 5 through repeated deletion of independent low-degree sets and retriangulation. The exact constants are less important than the invariant: each level is a smaller proxy that can route the query toward the full-resolution answer.

title: Extremal Polytope Query Roadmap
notes: Use this proof DAG as a roadmap rather than a full proof. The query descends through a small hierarchy, maintains a conflict or containing simplex, and returns to the original polytope with a support certificate. This is the conceptual bridge from convex polygon support to higher-dimensional polytope queries.

title: Planar Point Location
notes: Now the search target is not an extreme vertex but the cell containing a query point. The point-location DAG stores simple decisions, and the checked path uses three tests before reaching leaf T5. Connect this to the earlier predicate story: every node is still a geometric classification.

title: Randomized Trapezoidal Decomposition
notes: Present trapezoidal decomposition as a search-friendly refinement of a segment arrangement. Random insertion creates trapezoids and a decision structure using endpoint and segment-above tests. The notebook note that each trapezoid has bounded above and below neighbors is the geometric reason the structure stays navigable.

title: Recap And Lab Prompts
notes: Close by asking students to connect the chapter's repeated pattern. First classify a local event; then state the boundary convention; then use those events in a global structure. The lab prompts invite them to vary degeneracies, segment counts, support directions, and point-location queries while watching the checks fail or pass.
